d.t: A person, especially a large male, who is clumsy or a simpleton.
d.e: Ouch! You dropped that box on my feet, you lumbering oaf!

d.t: An ill-mannered person; a boor.
d.e: I hope you haven't been thinking me an awful oaf for not writing to thank you for so many jolly games after I left Tapsfield?

d.t: An elf's child; a changeling left by fairies or goblins, hence, a deformed or foolish child.
Characteristic of or resembling an oaf; clumsy, stupid.
d.e: "I don't wanter hyar uv nary one uv my gals bein' seen on airy street uv thisyer town, a-havin' no flirty flatter talk with thet wild Culberton younun!" was the popular edict that lazy, oafish fathers shot across dinner tables—as they packed down knivesful of baked chicken…

d.t: A deciduous tree with distinctive deeply lobed leaves, acorns, and notably strong wood, typically of England and northeastern North America, included in genus Quercus.
d.e: It was not far from the house; but the ground sank into a depression there, and the ridge of it behind shut out everything except just the roof of the tallest hayrick. As one sat on the sward behind the elm, with the back turned on the rick and nothing in front but the tall elms…

d.t: Any member of species of the genus Quercus, in family Fagaceae.
Any member of other species of trees resembling typical oaks of genus Quercus in some ways.
The outer (lockable) door of a set of rooms in a college or similar institution. (Often in the phrase sport one's oak.)
d.e: [E]very set of rooms has two doors, and I soon learned that the outer door, which is thick and solid, is called the oak, and to shut it is termed, to sport.

d.t: Having a rich brown color, like that of oak wood.
Made of oak wood or timber.
d.e: an oak table, oak beam, etc.

d.t: To expose to oak in order for the oak to impart its flavors.
Of a wine: aged in oak so that it acquires flavor from tannins in the wood.
Made from the wood of the oak tree. Also in metaphorical uses, suggesting robustness.
d.e: Captain Jemmy, taking up three bottles one after another and finding them all empty, ordered up three more, and drew his chair up to the hearth, where he sat kicking the oaken logs viciously with his long legs.

d.t: The leaf of an oak tree.
A device, badge or emblem shaped like the leaf of an oak, and indicating an award. (see Oak leaves)
Any of various nymphalid butterflies of the Asian genus Kallima.
Evernia prunastri, a lichen found primarily on oak trees and used in perfume.
d.e: He shellacked them with smoky labdanum, oakmoss and incense black as pitch.

d.t: A green color reminiscent of oakmoss.
A stakes race in which entry is restricted to 3-year-old fillies.
Coarse fibres separated by hackling from flax or hemp when preparing the latter for spinning.
Fibres chiefly obtained by untwisting old rope, which are used to caulk or pack gaps between boards of wooden ships and joints in masonry and plumbing, and sometimes for dressing wounds.
d.e: [W]ho should it be but Mr. Daniel, all muffled up, and his face as black as the chimney, and covered with dirt, pitch, and tarr, and powder, and muffled with dirty clouts, and his right eye stopped with okum. He is come last night at five o'clock from the fleete, with a comrade…

d.t: A wood populated with oak trees.
d.e: He says moreover the Earl of Galloway had an oakwood of three miles extent along the Cree, whence a great part of Wigtonshire is supplied with timber[…]

d.t: The wood of an oak tree.
d.e: Then I ran into the wilderness again of Wolf Creek, and spent 25 cents of the last little money I had in buying a can of salmon, which I devoured sitting on a log in the forest, and came at night to Grave Creek, and split a pile of oakwood, getting a good supper thereby and a…

d.t: Resembling or characteristic of the oak tree or its wood.
Describing the taste of wine that has been aged in oak and acquired tannins from the wood.

A type of lever used to propel a boat, having a flat blade at one end and a handle at the other, and pivoted in a rowlock atop the gunwale, whereby a rower seated in the boat and pulling the handle can pass the blade through the water by repeated strokes against the water's resistance, thus moving the boat.
d.e: The oar snaps in his hand Before he reaches dry land But the sound doesn't deafen his smile Just pokes at wet sand With an oar in his hand Floats off down the river Nile Floats off down the river Nile...

d.t: An oarsman; a rower.
d.e: He is a good oar.

d.t: An oar-like swimming organ of various invertebrates.
To row; to travel with, or as if with, oars.
d.e: The weather was fine, and whilst oaring along I would fain have landed on the islands between; but fearful of a change, and already half worn-out by my previous trail, I let them go by with the comforting resolve of turning them up on some future occasion.

d.t: Having oars.
A large, greatly elongated, type of fish of the family Regalecidae.
d.e: For the second time this year an oarfish, a rarely seen deep sea fish that has historically been considered a harbinger of doom, washed up on the California coastline.

d.t: A person who rows a boat, either alone or with others.
d.e: Davidson’s boat had steadied down and the bow oarsman, hurriedly peaking his oar by placing the end in a socket on the side of the boat opposite the thole-pins, had grabbed a harpoon and was bracing himself for the throw.

d.t: A coconut plantation.
A spring of fresh water, surrounded by a fertile region of vegetation, in a desert.
d.e: It was the Lost Oasis, the Oasis of the vision in the sand. […] Deep-hidden in the hollow, beneath the cliffs, it lay; and round it the happy verdure spread for many a rood. […] Yes, the quest was ended, the Lost Oasis was the Found!

d.t: A quiet, peaceful place or situation separated from surrounding noise or bustle.
d.e: The park was an oasis in the middle of the busy city.

d.t: A place or situation of fruitfulness or abundance separated from surrounding barrenness or scarcity.
d.e: [T]here is no true American music but the wild sweet melodies of the Negro slave; the American fairy tales and folklore are Indian and African; and, all in all, we black men seem the sole oasis of simple faith and reverence in a dusty desert of dollars and smartness.

d.t: A kiln for drying tobacco, malt and especially hops.
Widely cultivated cereal grass, typically Avena sativa.
d.e: The oat stalks made good straw.

d.t: Any of the numerous species, varieties, or cultivars of any of several similar grain plants in genus Avena.
d.e: The wild red oat is thought to be the ancestor of modern food oats.

d.t: The seeds of the oat, a grain, harvested as a food crop and for animal feed.
d.e: […]I could munch your good dry Oates. Me-thinkes I haue a great deſire to a bottle of hay: good hay, ſweete hay hath no fellow.

d.t: A simple musical pipe made of oat-straw.
The tiniest amount; a whit or jot.
d.e: Few of them care an oat for the niceties of the arrow sport, but for the young lords that may be on a hunt!

d.t: Any of many flat biscuits, or cakes, made from oatmeal.
Of, pertaining to, or made of oats.
d.e: an oaten cake

d.t: A solemn pledge or promise that invokes a deity, a ruler, or another entity (not necessarily present) to attest the truth of a statement or sincerity of one's desire to fulfill a contract or promise.
d.e: take an oath

d.t: A statement or promise which is strengthened (affirmed) by such a pledge.
d.e: After taking the oath of office, she became the country's forty-third premier.

d.t: A light, irreverent or insulting appeal to a deity or other entity.
A curse, a curse word.
d.e: The farther from the Senator's office, the darker and older the furniture, the freer fly four-letter oaths, the higher the heaps of unfiled and unattended papers culminating in a frenzy of pulp in the press section[…]

d.t: To pledge.
Someone who breaks an oath; a perjurer.
A police officer.
Meal made from rolled or round oats.
A breakfast cereal made from rolled oats, cooked in milk or water.
d.e: As we age, the major arteries of our bodies frequently become thickened with plaque, a fatty material with an oatmeal-like consistency that builds up along the inner lining of blood vessels. The reason plaque forms isn’t entirely known, but it seems to be related to high levels…

d.t: A light greyish brown colour, like that of oatmeal.
Of a light greyish brown colour, like that of oatmeal.
d.e: Boldly patterned textiles in oatmeal tones with a woven design in a strongly contrasting colour can be used alike for upholstery and as a wall hanging […]

d.t: A mass of oat plants (genus Avena, especially Avena sativa).
d.e: Oats are in the north corner of the farm.

d.t: Seeds of an oat plant, especially prepared as food.
d.e: Oats is a heart-healthy breakfast food.

d.t: Sexual intercourse, sexual satisfaction; semen.
d.e: Must I beat the Bush while you catch the Game ; Sow your wild oates, And mind not her wild notes, Of Alack &c. […] [She] bid me fill, fill, fill Her Sack &c. But twas all in Vaine For I had spilt my graine With a Thwack, &c.

d.t: Containing oats.
Resembling oats.
A semihard white cheese from the Oaxaca region of Mexico.
Relating to, or from, the Mexican state of Oaxaca.
d.e: Unsurprisingly, the Oaxacan cheese steak sandwich contains jalapeno peppers.

d.t: A native or inhabitant of the Mexican state of Oaxaca.
